mcqs.question: Why can't firmware just load the kernel directly, skipping the bootloader?
options: Firmware and bootloaders are actually the same program with two names
It's purely a legacy convention with no technical reason today
Firmware is deliberately kept minimal and generic, while finding, configuring, and loading a specific kernel (with a boot menu, initramfs, etc.) needs more capability than firmware provides
Kernels are physically too large to fit in the memory firmware can address
mcqs.explanation: Firmware stays minimal by design; the bootloader exists specifically to handle the more complex job of locating, configuring, and loading a kernel plus its supporting files. It's not merely legacy convention, firmware and bootloader are distinct programs, and kernel size relative to firmware's addressable memory isn't the actual constraint.

mcqs.question: A server boots from a 4TB disk using GPT partitioning with Secure Boot enabled. What firmware must it be using?
options: BIOS, since GPT and Secure Boot both work under legacy BIOS
UEFI, since BIOS can't address disks over ~2TB and has no Secure Boot capability
Neither — this configuration requires a custom firmware
It could be either, since both support all of these features identically
mcqs.explanation: A disk over 2TB with GPT partitioning and Secure Boot are both firmly UEFI-only capabilities — legacy BIOS has neither. No custom firmware is needed, and the two standards are not equivalent here.

mcqs.question: Why does the kernel use a temporary initramfs before mounting the real root filesystem?
options: The kernel might need drivers (e.g. for RAID or disk encryption) to reach the real root filesystem, and those drivers have to come from somewhere before it's mounted
It's a leftover step with no functional purpose on modern systems
The real root filesystem is always too large to mount directly at boot
It allows the user to edit kernel source code before the OS starts
mcqs.explanation: The initramfs solves a genuine chicken-and-egg problem: reaching an encrypted or RAID root disk may need a driver that isn't built into the kernel image itself, so a minimal temporary filesystem supplies it first. It's functionally necessary on many systems, unrelated to filesystem size, and has nothing to do with editing kernel source.

mcqs.question: What is the main practical advantage of systemd over traditional SysV init?
options: systemd uses less disk space than SysV init scripts
systemd removes the need for an init process entirely
systemd starts independent services in parallel based on an explicit dependency graph, rather than strictly sequentially
systemd only works on non-Linux operating systems
mcqs.explanation: systemd's declarative unit files express dependencies explicitly, letting it parallelize startup of independent services — a real boot-time win over SysV init's strictly sequential numbered scripts. It doesn't particularly save disk space, it is itself an init process (PID 1), and it's a Linux-specific system.

mcqs.question: A machine shows full, normal-looking kernel boot messages, then hangs and drops to an emergency shell partway through service startup. Which stage failed?
options: The bootloader failed to find the kernel
Firmware POST failed before any software ran
The kernel panicked during hardware initialization
Init or a specific service failed, since the kernel itself clearly started and handed off successfully
mcqs.explanation: Seeing full, normal kernel boot output means firmware, bootloader, and the kernel all succeeded — the failure is downstream, in init or a specific unit/service. A bootloader failure or kernel panic would show very different symptoms (no kernel output, or a panic message), and POST failing would prevent any of this from being visible at all.

mcqs.question: Why do containers start in milliseconds while a full VM typically takes 10-30+ seconds to boot?
options: Containers use faster CPUs than VMs by default
Containers skip firmware, bootloader, and kernel boot entirely, sharing the host's already-running kernel
VMs always run on slower physical storage than containers
Containers pre-load their entire application into a hardware cache before the request arrives
mcqs.explanation: A container doesn't boot an OS at all — it starts a process against a kernel the host already booted, skipping the entire firmware/bootloader/kernel-init chain a VM must go through. It's not about CPU speed, storage speed, or hardware caching — it's the boot chain itself being bypassed.
